power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Subjective experiences featuring altered self-awareness, temporal perception, or spatial boundaries-termed Non-Ordinary Experiences (NOEs)-occur across clinical neurology, psychiatry, and psychedelic medicine, including in insular ecstatic seizures, meditation, breathwork, hypnosis, and psychedelic therapy.
Objective:
To synthesize neurobiological and clinical literature on NOEs for neurologists by presenting three heuristic frameworks: 1.
A six-dimension phenomenological taxonomy; 2.
A tri-level descriptive taxonomy (computational "software", neuromodulatory-autonomic "firmware", and network "hardware"); 3.

The Trigger-Dynamic Psyche-4E Appraisal-Outcome Model, which maps how acute neurodynamic shifts resolve into adaptive growth or clinical distress without reducing existential meaning to neural activity.
Narrative synthesis of systematic reviews, coordinate-based meta-analyses, and key theoretical frameworks sourced via PubMed/MEDLINE.
Conflating spirituality, religion, and NOEs causes construct contamination in neuroimaging, compounded by unvalidated single-item measures and non-independent cohorts.

An fMRI metaanalysis of meditation (34 studies, N=700) reveals aggregate recruitment of the right rolandic operculum, left insula, supplementary motor area, and hippocampus, arguing against a singular "spiritual center".
First-person reports are mapped using a six-dimension schema (experiential content, temporal dynamics, spatial dynamics, volitional dynamics/agency, ownership/embodiment, cognitive stance).

Mechanistically, states are organized across three bidirectionally coupled levels: computational inference ("software"), neuromodulatory-autonomic state-setting ("firmware"), and large-scale networks ("hardware").

Five entry routes (meditation, psychedelics, breathwork, hypnosis, focal neurological events) are hypothesized to share shifts in Bayesian precision weighting and network decoupling within the master Trigger-Dynamic Psyche-4E Appraisal-Outcome Model.

Crucially, long-term outcomes (integration vs. distress) are not dictated by acute brain states alone, but are mediated by contextual filtering through the 4E Appraisal Prism (embodied, embedded, enacted, extended dimensions).
Neurospirituality bridges network neuroscience, clinical neurology, and person-centered care.
Clarifying biological substrates does not resolve existential validity.

Clinicians must maintain a strict distinction between biological mechanisms, subjective experiences, and personal meanings (the Epistemological Invariant) to avoid pathologizing adaptive states or romanticizing neurological disease.
The scientific investigation of spiritual and transcendent experiences possesses a deep history, evolving from early localizationist hypotheses into modern network neuroscience.
Early phrenological attempts, such as Franz Gall's mapping of spiritual organs, sought biological substrates for transcendence but lacked empirical validity.

The phenomenological foundation was established by William James, who demonstrated that first-person qualitative reports could be systematically analyzed as empirical psychological data (as reviewed in Harper, 2019).

text.text: Concurrently, early psychoanalytic paradigms offered contrasting interpretations of the "oceanic feeling": Sigmund Freud, in Civilization and Its Discontents (1930), framed it as a regressive preservation of infantile narcissism, whereas Carl Jung (1969) viewed such transcendent states as transformative encounters with archetypal structures essential to psychological individuation (both cited and discussed in Unterrainer, 2025).

text.text: These foundational perspectives established an enduring conceptual tension between biological reductionism and spiritual transcendence.
Terminology in this field evolved alongside its empirical methodologies.
The term "neurotheology," initially appearing in fiction by Aldous Huxley, was formalized into an academic framework by James Ashbrook in the 1980s.

A decisive empirical milestone occurred at the turn of the millennium, when Andrew Newberg and Eugene d'Aquili utilized SPECT imaging to measure regional cerebral blood flow shifts during meditation and prayer (Newberg et al., 2001; Newberg et al., 2003).

text.text: Over the subsequent two decades, the discipline shifted away from basic localizationism toward large-scale network neuroscience-focusing on dynamic interactions among the Default Mode Network (DMN), Salience Network (SN), and Central Executive Network (CEN)-complemented by 4E cognition (embodied, embedded, enacted, and extended frameworks) (Harper, 2019; McNamara & Grafman, 2024; Jedlicka & Havenith, 2025; Timmermann et al., 2023; Unterrainer, 2025).

text.text: To maintain scientific precision, three frequently conflated terms must be explicitly demarcated: • Neuroscience of religion and spirituality: Basic empirical research investigating the neural and cognitive correlates of spiritual phenomena.
• Neurotheology: An interdisciplinary hermeneutic enterprise synthesizing neuroscientific findings with theological and philosophical frameworks.

• Neurospirituality: A translational clinical framework grounded in personcentered healthcare and palliative medicine, applying neuroscientific insights directly to the existential and spiritual dimensions of patient care, particularly within clinical neurology (da Mota Gomes, 2024; da Mota Gomes et al., 2026).

text.text: Differentiating these domains prevents category errors, such as deriving direct clinical management protocols from raw neuroimaging correlations.
To integrate these disparate literatures into clinical practice, this review advances three original heuristic contributions, each offered as a conceptual device pending formal validation: 1.

The Six Phenomenological Dimensions of Non-Ordinary Experiences (NOEs): An operationalized descriptive schema extending the neurophenomenological work of Timmermann et al. (2023) to categorize first-person qualitative reports along six dimensions (experiential content, temporal dynamics, spatial dynamics, volitional dynamics/agency, ownership/embodiment, and cognitive stance), without reducing experience to biological mechanisms.

The computational designations serve strictly as a heuristic mnemonic and pragmatic organizing device-not as a literal computer architecture or a dualistic separation of mind and brain.

Central to this overarching architecture is an Epistemological Invariant: mapping the biological mechanism of a transcendent state constrains its physical substrate but does not dictate its existential validity or personal meaning.
A detailed operationalization of this model and its six-step clinical reasoning heuristic is provided in Section 5 and Section 5.6.

text.text: Conceptual Foundations
text.formatted: Conceptual Foundations</head>

text.text: Four terminological commitments establish the conceptual foundation for this review, beginning with a deliberate choice of nomenclature.

This review prefers neurospirituality over the neuroscience of religion because NOEs are not inherently religious: an experience of ego dissolution, oceanic boundlessness, or ecstatic certainty may be interpreted religiously, spiritually, secularly, or not interpreted at all.

The term is religion-neutral by design-neutral with respect to religion, not opposed to it-able to accommodate religious framing without requiring it and secular framing without excluding the religious.
That neutrality is what makes the vocabulary usable across theistic, non-theistic, and culturally diverse clinical settings.
The remaining commitments concern what the words mean.

Spirituality, as used here, is a meaning-making orientation involving perceived connection to something beyond the individual self-transcendent (the divine, the sacred), natural, interpersonal, or a blend of these.
For a secular patient, "beyond self" may mean community, nature, or future generations rather than God; the formulation holds either way.
Religion refers to the organized beliefs, rituals, doctrines, and communities through which many people express their spirituality.

The two overlap heavily-spiritual experiences happen inside religious traditions, and religious life involves far more than doctrine-but they are not the same thing, and the habit of collapsing them into a single "S/R" measure, pervasive in the neuroimaging literature, makes it impossible to know which dimension is actually driving which neural outcome (Rosmarin et al., 2022; Maraldi et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The two overlap heavily-spiritual experiences happen inside religious traditions, and religious life involves far more than doctrine-but they are not the same thing, and the habit of collapsing them into a single "S/R" measure, pervasive in the neuroimaging literature, makes it impossible to know which dimension is actually driving which neural outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Rosmarin et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Maraldi et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Two further distinctions are maintained throughout, because the clinical recommendations of this review depend on them.

Spirituality is treated as a disposition-for the purpose of choosing instruments, a relatively enduring orientation-whereas spiritual well-being is a state: the felt sense of alignment with whatever a person holds as personally, communally, or transcendentally significant.
The former is the broader construct; the latter is what the clinician actually assesses and what outcomes research measures.

And spiritual meaning (connection to something perceived as sacred or beyond the self) is distinguished from existential meaning (purpose, dignity, and value drawn from secular sourcesrelationships, work, legacy).
Existential suffering can occur without any spirituality at all, which is why the clinician should assess existential concerns regardless of the patient's spiritual identification.
These definitions are pragmatic, adopted because they can be operationalized in clinical neuroscience-not because they claim cross-cultural validity.

They reflect a largely Western, Christian-inflected understanding of spirituality; other traditions conceptualize the territory differently, as interconnectedness with ancestors in Ubuntu philosophy, harmony with cosmic order in Indigenous frameworks, or alignment with natural forces in Taoist and Buddhist thought.
The definitions earn their keep by making measurement possible, and spiritual assessment should always proceed with cultural humility.

NOEs are defined phenomenologically rather than etiologically: subjective experiences involving identifiable alterations in the content, organization, or sense of self of consciousness, relative to a person's ordinary waking state.
The category gathers mystical, transcendent, oceanic, ecstatic, and psychedelic states, together with selected experiences arising from hypnosis, meditation, breathwork, and neurological conditions.
It is a descriptive umbrella, not a claim about mechanism.
Nothing about inclusion implies a shared cause, an equivalence of phenomenology, or a comparable fate.
Three qualifications carry through everything that follows.
NOEs are not inherently pathological, though some occur alongside psychiatric or neurological illness.
They are not synonymous with spiritual or religious experience, since unusual experiences arrive without spiritual interpretation all the time.
And they are not homogeneous: their phenomenology, significance, and consequences differ profoundly across contexts (Timmermann et al., 2023; Maraldi et al., 2024).

text.text: For analytical purposes, it helps to distinguish four levels that are related but never interchangeable: enduring dispositions and orientations toward meaning and the sacred; the practices and contexts in which these find expression, from prayer to psychoactive substances; the particular experiential episodes themselves; and the interpretations and consequences that follow.
These levels interact over time-prior beliefs shape how an experience is read, and experiences in turn reshape beliefs-but neither direction of influence should be assumed in advance.
A deeply spiritual person may never report an NOE; a diehard materialist may have one and be shaken by it.
The distinction is conceptual separability, not a demonstration of statistical independence.

To compare non-ordinary experiences across diverse contexts without flattening their unique features, the six phenomenological dimensions taxonomy synthetically extends Timmermann et al. (2023) across six analytical axes: experiential content (sensory, imagistic, and affective qualities), temporal dynamics (felt duration, flow, and continuity), spatial dynamics (distance, extension, and boundaries), volitional dynamics or agency (authorship and control over thoughts and actions), ownership, embodiment, and self-experience (running from ordinary bodily ownership to radical self-dissolution), and cognitive stance (the fused, detached, or meta-aware relation to ongoing thoughts).

text.text: Offered as a shared descriptive vocabulary rather than a set of established orthogonal variables, this framework systematically specifies phenomenological shifts without assuming fixed valence or structural conflation.

The instrument that comes closest to this comparative ambition-though it realizes it only partially-is the Altered States of Consciousness (ASC) rating-scale family, whose etiology-independent design and broad experiential coverage make it the most comprehensive validated instrument currently available.

Its most recent revalidation, the 3D-ASCr (Stocker et al., 2026), integrates eleven lower-order subscales (42 items) into three coherent higher-order dimensions: Positive Effects (PosE), Distressing Effects (DisE), and Perceptual Effects (PerE).
text.formatted: Its most recent revalidation, the 3D-ASCr <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Stocker et al., 2026)</ref>, integrates eleven lower-order subscales (42 items) into three coherent higher-order dimensions: Positive Effects (PosE), Distressing Effects (DisE), and Perceptual Effects (PerE).

text.text: This hierarchical structure organizes experience by valence and content-positively valenced and meaningful experiences, distressing states, and perceptual phenomena-and is validated for classic serotonergic psychedelics across a wide dose range, with its dimensions closely approximating Dittrich's original OB, AED, and VR.
A dimension-by-dimension comparison, however, reveals that even this instrument covers only part of the sixfold space.

It provides strong coverage of experiential content and substantial coverage of ownership, embodiment, and self-experience, but captures volitional dynamics only in their negative pole (impaired control), leaving the graded exercise of agency unmeasured; temporal and spatial dynamics fare worst, surviving only as indirect traces; and no subscale operationalizes cognitive stance as the relation to ongoing thought.

This asymmetry generalizes to the other major multidimensional instruments-the PES48 and the Hallucinogen Rating Scale-whose shared tripartite structure likewise organizes experience by valence and content rather than by structure, and to narrower single-construct tools (EDI, MEQ30, PCI), each of which captures only one pole or one fused facet of the structural axes.
The comparison thus yields a precise division of labor.
The ASC family offers what the sixfold schema deliberately does not: quantified, psychometrically validated, outcomelinked measurement.

Conversely, the six-dimension taxonomy offers what no current instrument provides: systematic, valence-free coverage of the structural axes-graded agency, felt time and space, and cognitive stance-that cut across the valence-based domains of the validated scales.

Neither substitutes for the other: validated instruments serve as mandatory anchors for quantification, while the sixfold schema functions as the common descriptive vocabulary into which their subscales can be translated-the precondition for linking phenomenological report and neural measurement on a single, explicit map.
To demonstrate the qualitative utility of this schema, Box 1 applies these parameters to three contrasting historical and literary reports.
A note for readers: Box 1 only illustrates how the six dimensions can be used to describe an experience.
The schema was built partly to fit classical accounts, so the box is not evidence for the schema or for any brain mechanism.
To illustrate how the six-dimension schema operationalizes first-person reports without reducing them to biological mechanisms, three contrasting cases are benchmarked below.
These accounts serve strictly as qualitative demonstrations of descriptive classification-not as empirical biological proof.
The three cases were deliberately selected for contrast across induction vectors; the selection was not systematic and confers no evidential weight on the schema itself.
Case A: Marguerite Porete (Âme Anéantie) -Primary and secondary sources: Porete, The Mirror of Simple Souls (c. 1300); Mieth (2025).

text.text: Marguerite Porete, a 14th-century Beguine mystic executed for heresy in 1310, described in The Mirror of Simple Souls the soul's total annihilation in divine love (âme anéantie)-a state of loving "without why" (sans pourquoi) that surrenders individual self-will.
Mapped onto the framework: • Ownership and Embodiment: Radical dissolution of personal self-identity and self-will.
• Volitional Dynamics: Deliberate surrender of agency, rather than involuntary loss of control.
• Cognitive Stance: Complete detachment from egoic self-narratives (parallel to Meister Eckhart's Abgeschiedenheit; Mieth, 2025).

text.text: The ecstatic aura is attested in two distinct kinds of sources, which should be kept apart.
The first is fiction: in The Idiot, Prince Myshkin recounts moments of sublime harmony and beauty culminating in an "ecstatic, prayerful merging with the highest synthesis of life."
This is a fictional character's account, not direct testimony from Dostoevsky.
The second is secondary biographical and medical literature (e.g., Gschwind & Picard, 2016), which attributes similar experiences to Dostoevsky's own seizures.
text.formatted: The second is secondary biographical and medical literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Gschwind & Picard, 2016)</ref>, which attributes similar experiences to Dostoevsky's own seizures.

text.text: Because that attribution is retrospective, the epilepsy diagnosis rests on historical reconstruction rather than clinical examination, and the literature variously describes the condition as temporal lobe epilepsy and as insular or ecstatic epilepsy.
Mapped onto the schema: • Experiential Content: Intense, overwhelming feelings of bliss, serenity, and inner wholeness.
• Cognitive Stance: Absolute subjective certainty and clarity without rational doubt.
• Temporal Dynamics: Subjective time dilation and a collapse of felt duration into expanded present-moment awareness.
• Neurobiological Context: Ecstatic seizures are proposed to originate in a network centered on the anterior insular cortex.

On the zero-error hypothesis of Picard and Friston (2014), hyper-synchronous epileptic discharge may disrupt the insular comparator that evaluates incoming sensory signals against predictions, transiently suppressing prediction-error generation and locking the brain into an artificial, zero-error "stable state" experienced as certainty and bliss (Picard & Friston, 2014; Gschwind & Picard, 2016).

text.text: In his 1927 correspondence with Sigmund Freud, the French writer Romain Rolland described the "oceanic feeling" as a simple, direct feeling of the "eternal"-an unmediated sensation of limitless, boundless oneness with the whole universe (as analyzed in Maharaj, 2017).

text.text: Mapped onto the framework: • Spatial Dynamics: Vast, unconstrained spatial expansion without perceptible limits.
• Temporal Dynamics: Time experienced as timelessness, as "the eternal."
• Ownership and Embodiment: Dissolution of rigid egoic boundaries into total cosmic unity.
• Cognitive Stance: A direct intuitive stance wholly independent of formal religious dogma, credos, church organizations, or sacred texts.
• Experiential Content and Affective Tone: A spontaneous state experienced as a constant source of vital renewal and energy.
• Methodological Caution: Rolland's report illustrates secular or non-dogmatic selftranscendence and shows how ego boundaries loosen in a specific first-person account.
A single anecdotal report, however, cannot demonstrate that ego boundaries loosen without clinical distress as a general rule.

Takeaway and Comparative Summary: Comparing contemplative surrender (Porete), focal epileptic discharges (Dostoevsky), and spontaneous mystical report (Rolland) shows that identical phenomenological signatures-bliss, time dilation, boundary dissolution-can emerge across contexts while their induction vectors and clinical trajectories remain fundamentally distinct.
Ego dissolution occurs in monasteries, in psychedelic sessions, and on psychiatric wards.
The descriptions can be strikingly similar; the fates are not.
Two people may report a diminished sense of self while differing in bodily awareness, agency, emotional tone, and functional capacity, and the same label may prescribe entirely different courses.

Phenomenological comparison is therefore necessary, but never sufficient for judging causal or clinical equivalence, and outcomes cannot be sorted into a tidy binary of growth versus pathology-a single experience can carry both benefit and harm, and its meaning may be renegotiated for years afterward (Maraldi et al., 2024).

text.text: What tends to matter for the trajectory is not the content of the experience but its context: pre-existing psychological resources, social support, expectations, interpretive frameworks, and how the experience is ultimately woven into a life.
These are candidate moderators and mediators of outcome-variables that do not alter the acute neurodynamic state itself, but shape what that state comes to mean and what it leaves behind.

The 4E Prism therefore operates at two analytically distinct points: it shapes the acute state through set and setting (as the empirical literature on contextual modulation of psychedelic and meditative states documents), and it filters the aftermath through appraisal and integration.

text.text: The same neurodynamic perturbation does not travel directly to a uniform outcome.

It passes through what the integrative model terms the 4E Appraisal Prism-embodied, embedded, enacted, and extended-a contextual filter whose candidate metrics (baseline HRV, interoceptive accuracy, set-and-setting inventories, and semantic coping frameworks) are proposed but have not yet been used in any study to predict NOE outcomes and remain strictly candidate proxies.
(See Figure 3 in Section 5 for the complete stage-by-stage flow diagram of this architecture.)
This has a methodological consequence that runs through the rest of the review.
If context is constitutive, then studies reporting only the trigger and the outcome-psychedelic dose and symptom change, meditation hours and well-being score-are systematically underdetermined.
They cannot explain why identical interventions produce heterogeneous results, and they cannot identify the moderators that prospective designs should measure.
The candidate moderators listed above are therefore not incidental covariates; they are the variables the 4E Appraisal Prism is designed to operationalize.

Until they are measured directly-through baseline heart rate variability, interoceptive accuracy tasks, set-and-setting inventories, and semantic coping frameworks-the field will continue to confuse similar phenomenology with identical trajectories, and will continue to mistake the content of an experience for its cause (Jedlicka & Havenith, 2025; Maraldi et al., 2024; Timmermann et al., 2023; Unterrainer, 2025).

text.text: Neural mechanism, phenomenal experience, and existential meaning are distinct levels of analysis.
Finding the neural correlate of an experience constrains its physical substrate; it does not tell us what the experience was like for the person, and it settles nothing about its significance.
The intensity of an experience, conversely, is not evidence for any particular mechanism, let alone for a metaphysical conclusion.

This review rejects both directions of overreach with equal force: neurobiological reductionism, in which a brain description is treated as settling every existential question, and its mirror image, in which the felt meaning of an experience is taken as evidence about biology or metaphysics (Jedlicka & Havenith, 2025).
text.formatted: This review rejects both directions of overreach with equal force: neurobiological reductionism, in which a brain description is treated as settling every existential question, and its mirror image, in which the felt meaning of an experience is taken as evidence about biology or metaphysics <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Jedlicka & Havenith, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The distinction does not make the levels causally independent-brain states contribute to the conditions of experience, experiences alter beliefs, beliefs alter attention and memory-but it does mean that each level must be investigated with methods suited to it.
One sentence, repeated at the close of this review, captures the commitment: causal mechanism is not phenomenological experience, and phenomenological experience is not spiritual meaning.
This invariant is not only a philosophical commitment; it is a clinical instruction.
At the bedside, it requires the clinician to assess three things separately:
The mechanism: what is happening in the brain and body (e.g., anterior insular discharge in ecstatic epilepsy).
• The experience: what the patient reports phenomenologically (e.g., feelings of absolute unity and bliss).
• The meaning: what the patient takes the experience to signify existentially or spiritually.
Collapsing any two of these produces a characteristic error-reducing a meaningful experience to discharge activity, or inflating a neural correlate into a metaphysical proof.
As demonstrated in Dostoevsky's case (Box 1), a neurological patient's report of transcendent bliss is neither reducible to discharge pathology nor evidence of metaphysical contact.
It is a phenomenological event with a constraining biological substrate-and the patient requires clinical neurological care for epilepsy regardless of how the aura is personally interpreted.
Mechanism, experience, and meaning hold their distinct places even at the moment they seem most entangled.
"Oceanic states"-defined by ego dissolution, felt unity, and timelessness-exist at the intersection of psychopathology, artistic expression, and self-transcendence.
The concept originated in a 1927 letter from Romain Rolland to Sigmund Freud following the publication of Freud's The Future of an Illusion (as discussed in Maharaj, 2017).

text.text: Rolland described a spontaneous "oceanic" feeling of limitless oneness with the universe, existing independently of dogmas or church structures.
Citing Sri Ramakrishna and Swami Vivekananda, Rolland maintained that oceanic states foster dynamic action and intellectual vigor rather than psychological regression.

Conversely, Freud dismissed the experience in Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) as a regressive illusion rooted in infantile narcissism and pre-Oedipal helplessness (Freud, 1930 , as cited in Unterrainer, 2025).
text.formatted: Conversely, Freud dismissed the experience in Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) as a regressive illusion rooted in infantile narcissism and pre-Oedipal helplessness <ref type="bibr">(Freud, 1930</ref> <ref type="bibr">, as cited in Unterrainer, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Re-examining Rolland's biographies Vie de Ramakrishna (1929) and Vie de Vivekananda (1930), Ayon Maharaj (2017) demonstrates that Rolland's primary intent was not to solicit a psychoanalytic validation of mysticism, but to challenge psychoanalytic reductionism directly.

text.text: Rolland leveled three core critiques against psychoanalysis: first, an extroverted bias that pathologizes mystic introversion, thereby losing what Plotinus termed the "function of the real"; second, the misapplication of clinical regression theories (e.g., Théodule Ribot) to mystics, conflating infantile pre-discursive intuition with mystical post-discursive intuition (Édouard Le Roy, as cited in Maharaj, 2017 and Unterrainer, 2025)-a conflation later formalized by Ken Wilber as the "pre/trans fallacy"; and third, a superficial model of the unconscious that reduces transcendent states to sexual repression or Oedipal dynamics while ignoring the underlying "Ocean of Being" (l'Être océanique). Maharaj (2017) clarifies that scholars like William Parsons misread Rolland's phrase psychophysiologie mystique ("mystical psychophysiology") as an endorsement of "mystical psychoanalysis."

text.text: In truth, Rolland rejected psychoanalysis in favor of a Yogic "new science of the mind" (une nouvelle science de l'esprit).

Drawing on Patanjali's Rāja-Yoga (particularly pratyāhāra or detached observation) and Vedāntic Jñāna-Yoga-later modernized by Vivekananda and Sri Aurobindo-Rolland framed mystic introversion as an empirical method grounded in the Plotinian identity of seer and seen.

This critique presaged major twentieth-century transpersonal frameworks: Sri Aurobindo criticized psychoanalysis for attempting to explain the "superconscient" lotus purely through subconscious "mud"; Swami Akhilananda (1948, as cited in Unterrainer, 2025) advocated Yogic concentration over pathologizing clinical generalizations; and Ken Wilber exposed Freud's reduction of transrational states to prepersonal adualism as a classic pre/trans fallacy.

Beyond Freudian reductionism, Carl Jung (1969, as cited in Unterrainer, 2025) reinterpreted ego dissolution as a transformative encounter with the collective unconscious mediated by the numinosum (mysterium tremendum et fascinans).

In art theory, Anton Ehrenzweig (1967, as cited in Unterrainer, 2025) described oceanic feeling as a "de-differentiated perception" enabling creative "bisociation" (Arthur Koestler), a liminal space balancing visionary insight against psychic breakdown, as illustrated by Vincent van Gogh, Louis Wain, and Antonin Artaud.

Existential and Eastern philosophies ground these states further: ego dissolution manifests as a confrontation with existential nothingness (Jean-Paul Sartre, 1956, as discussed in Unterrainer, 2025), an authentic disclosure of Being through a rupture in Dasein (Martin Heidegger, 1962, as discussed in Unterrainer, 2025), or a return to primordial embodied unity (Maurice Merleau-Ponty, 2002, as discussed in Unterrainer, 2025), echoing Buddhist anattā and contemporary self-model theory (Thomas Metzinger, 2003 , as discussed in Unterrainer, 2025).

text.text: From an existential-neuroscience perspective, Unterrainer (2025) frames oceanic states as a dynamic reorganization of self-processing networks rather than brain dysfunction.

Cortically, ego dissolution correlates with functional decoupling within the DMN (mPFC, PCC, precuneus, angular gyrus), conceptualized as belief relaxation under the REBUS (Carhart-Harris & Friston, 2019) and ALBUS (Safron et al., 2025)   Unterrainer, 2025).

text.text: The neurobiological literature on NOEs is scattered across imaging, pharmacology, electrophysiology, and computation.
To hold it together, this review uses a three-level descriptive heuristic, coupled bidirectionally with phenomenal consciousness.
The gloss is an analogy, a pragmatic organizing device, not a literal architecture, and emphatically not a veiled dualism of mind and brain.
The three levels are levels of description, not levels of causation: they name three vocabularies in which the same system can be described, not three substances or three independent causal strata.

The bidirectional coupling between them is what prevents the metaphor from hardening into a hierarchy: repeated engagement may induce plastic changes in neural tissue, which alter neuromodulatory dynamics; the computational description then changes accordingly.
This is why psychosocial contextappraisal, setting, meaning-making-can have biological consequences rather than merely interpretive ones.

The first level, the network substrate, is the physical infrastructure: the triple-network architecture of DMN, SN, and CEN, within which the self is best conceived not as a thing but as an emergent, ongoing process of network interaction (Menon, 2011).

text.text: Thalamic gating, insular hubs, and subcortical structures provide entry points that constrain how the cortical networks configure themselves (Picard & Friston, 2014; Dost et al., 2025; Unterrainer, 2025).
text.formatted: Thalamic gating, insular hubs, and subcortical structures provide entry points that constrain how the cortical networks configure themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Picard & Friston, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Dost et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Unterrainer, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: McNamara and Grafman (2024) extend this picture to religious experience specifically, proposing that such experiences involve repeated cycles through salience, default mode, and frontoparietal evaluation, with the salience network acting as the switch-a dynamic picture compatible with everything argued here.
The second level, neuromodulatory and autonomic state-setting, comprises the systems that tune the network substrate.

Brainstem arousal networks and vagal afferents set baseline readiness and interoceptive tone; vagal tone, indexed by heart rate variability, tracks emotion regulation capacity and is hypothesized-though not established-to moderate the valence of non-ordinary states: a body that feels safe may be more open to surrender, a body on alert more prone to panic.
A distinction must be maintained here, because the literature routinely conflates two dissociable variables.

Resting vagal tone-measured at baseline, before any induction-is a trait variable: it indexes pre-existing autonomic flexibility and belongs analytically to the appraisal stage, where it is hypothesized to predict how an experience will be met and integrated.

Phasic HRV change during the experience itself is a state variable: it is a state-setting signature of the acute neurodynamic perturbation, and it may transiently decrease under sympathetic surge or vagal withdrawal.
However, because HRV is often reported to increase during slow-paced breathing and certain meditation practices, reduced HRV cannot be listed as a general feature of non-ordinary states.
The two are not interchangeable, and treating them as a single "HRV" measure obscures precisely the dissociation the model needs.

This is not a measurement artifact: systematic reviews of trait mindfulness report consistent trait-level neural correlates-amygdala reactivity, insular thickness, DMN connectivity-alongside inconsistent state-level EEG and between-network findings (Treves et al., 2024; Calderone et al., 2024).

text.text: The divergence between trait and state is therefore a feature of the underlying physiology, not a failure of the instruments.

Serotonergic 5-HT2A activation raises cortical signal entropy, while dopaminergic signalling determines which of the newly available states get flagged as salient and significant-an interaction that may explain why psychedelic experiences are at once so meaningful and so different from person to person (Carhart-Harris & Friston, 2019).

text.text: And the periaqueductal gray, classically studied for pain and defense, has emerged from lesion-network mapping as a node of unexpected breadth, implicated in carerelated affect, awe, and trait spirituality: a structure operating at the most basic embodied level, where the boundary between self and world, safety and surrender, can be radically redrawn (Unterrainer, 2025).

text.text: This characterization of the PAG, including its role as a node between embodiment and transcendence, is an interpretive extension resting on lesionnetwork mapping and a single review; it is a hypothesis, not an established finding.

At the level of computational inference, the brain functions as a predictive processing network, generating top-down expectations that interpret incoming bottom-up sensory signals, with neuromodulatory gain control adjusting the balance between expectation and evidence.

Within this framework, the REBUS model (Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics) proposes that 5-HT2A receptor activation weakens high-level cognitive expectations, flattening cortical hierarchies and allowing unconstrained sensory information to flood awareness.
Rather than a proven mechanism, REBUS remains a testable hypothesis with domain-specific and dose-dependent empirical support.

Addressing these limitations, the ALBUS model (Altered Beliefs Under Psychedelics) suggests that high-level expectations are not solely relaxed under psychedelics; they can also be amplified and entrenched through a complementary process termed SEBUS (Strengthened Beliefs Under Psychedelics).
Crucially, ALBUS positions context-including dose, mindset, and clinical environmentas a primary variable determining whether cognitive expectations loosen or harden.

While ALBUS and SEBUS were originally formulated for psychedelic compounds, extending this framework to non-pharmacological interventions such as meditation, hypnosis, or breathwork represents a broader theoretical generalization.

From a clinical and neuroscientific standpoint, REBUS, ALBUS/SEBUS, and related computational accounts-such as Picard and Friston's zero-error hypothesis-must be evaluated as heuristic models rather than confirmed pathophysiological mechanisms.
To avoid circular reasoning where any observed outcome fits the framework, these models require clear, falsifiable parameters.

Specifically, directionality must be pre-specified based on baseline clinical variables: for instance, high affective threat and rigid baseline priors should explicitly predict SEBUS-type belief strengthening, whereas supportive environments and high interoceptive accuracy predict REBUS-type relaxation.

Ultimately, these computational theories require the same empirical rigor applied to clinical neuroimaging, including construct validation, independent dataset replication, blinding, and systematic auditing before they can be accepted as established neurobiological facts.

Each level invites its own methods-connectivity analysis for the network substrate, pharmacology and autonomic measurement for the state-setting level, computational modeling for the inference level-and the coupling between them runs both ways.

Repeated engagement may induce plastic changes in neural tissue, which alter neuromodulatory dynamics; the computational description then changes accordingly: a recursive loop that is a plausible candidate mechanism for the durable effects of contemplative practice and psychedelic therapy.

text.text: The quantitative benchmark in contemplative neuroimaging derives from Baten et al. (2026), whose whole-brain coordinate-based fMRI meta-analysis synthesized 34 unique studies (N=700) across four practice families: focused attention, open monitoring, mantra recitation, and loving-kindness.
text.formatted: The quantitative benchmark in contemplative neuroimaging derives from <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Baten et al. (2026)</ref>, whose whole-brain coordinate-based fMRI meta-analysis synthesized 34 unique studies (N=700) across four practice families: focused attention, open monitoring, mantra recitation, and loving-kindness.

text.text: Across this aggregate dataset, meditation consistently recruits a core neural substrate comprising the right Rolandic operculum, left insula, right superior temporal gyrus, left supplementary motor area, and right hippocampus/parahippocampal gyrus.

Functional decoding links this substrate to interoceptive processing, self-monitoring, and cognitive reappraisal alongside reduced visual-perceptual loading, reflecting a systematic neural shift away from external sensory processing toward internal awareness.
Beyond this shared core, distinct practices exhibit tailored functional signatures.
Focused attention hyperactivates the left insula, bilateral supplementary motor area, right hippocampus, and right superior frontal gyrus while hypoactivating the right middle cingulate cortex.
Open monitoring recruits the left Rolandic operculum/insula, left middle temporal gyrus, left inferior frontal gyrus, and left superior frontal gyrus, accompanied by left thalamic hypoactivation.
Mantra recitation selectively engages the right putamen and insula, whereas loving-kindness recruits prefrontal networks, the anterior cingulate cortex, and the cerebellum.
This functional divergence provides empirical evidence against naive neurolocalizationism or a singular "spiritual center."

However, applying a symmetrical skeptical standard requires acknowledging that this foundational meta-analysis carries its own methodological constraints-namely, reliance on coordinate-based spatial estimates, task heterogeneity across primary paradigms, and modest sample sizes within specific practice sub-cells-which compound broader field-wide limitations such as varying practitioner expertise, heterogeneous control conditions, and unassessed publication bias (Calderone et al., 2024).

text.text: These empirical data further qualify network-level generalizations regarding DMN dynamics.

Although Baten et al. (2026) demonstrate consistent engagement of insular, opercular, motor, and hippocampal nodes, their findings do not establish global DMN decoupling as a universal neural signature of meditation.

text.text: Instead, involvement of DMNadjacent structures reflects dynamic attentional state fluctuations intrinsic to meditationparticularly during focused attention-as well as subtle subsystem variations between practice styles.
Broader claims regarding meditation-induced DMN decoupling must therefore be interpreted within these explicit functional boundaries.

If the meditation literature is young and still methodologically limited (Section 4.1), the spirituality-and-religion imaging literature is methodologically immature and subject to high risk of bias. (2022) systematically reviewed 18 neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies of S/R, mental health, and neurobiology, and what they found should unsettle anyone citing this literature as established.

text.text: What looks like a broad evidence base is, on inspection, largely one dataset counted several times, from a sample selected for depression risk that may not represent anyone else.

The celebrated association between personal religiosity and cortical thickness reported by Miller et al. (2014)-which demonstrated greater regional thickness in parietal and occipital cortices among adults at high familial risk for major depression (N=103; 67 high-risk, 36 low-risk)-rests on a single multi-generational lineage (the Columbia/Weissman cohort).

text.text: Because key neuroimaging and clinical reports in this line of literature draw from this same underlying participant pool, their overlapping sample base limits their status as fully autonomous corroborations, plausibly weakening the overall evidentiary base.
Crucially, however, dataset non-independence does not demonstrate that Miller et al.'s primary neuroanatomical finding is an artifact.
Rather, it shows that the finding has not yet been independently replicated in an autonomous cohort.
The distinction matters: an unreplicated finding may well be valid, and the appropriate scientific response is prospective replication in independent populations, not summary dismissal.
The measurement situation is no better, and the numbers deserve to be stated plainly.

Of the eighteen studies reviewed by Rosmarin et al. (2022), only three used psychometrically validated, multidimensional instruments-the Daily Spiritual Experiences Scale, the TCI-R Self-Transcendence subscale, or the DUREL.
text.formatted: Of the eighteen studies reviewed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Rosmarin et al. (2022)</ref>, only three used psychometrically validated, multidimensional instruments-the Daily Spiritual Experiences Scale, the TCI-R Self-Transcendence subscale, or the DUREL.

text.text: Eight relied on unvalidated single-item selfreports assessing general "importance of religion," five measured external religious attendance alone, and the remaining two relied on unvalidated, study-specific questionnaires or experimental prayer paradigms.

The consequence is that the regressor labeled "religiosity" or "spirituality" in most of this literature is not a construct but a placeholder-and there is no way to know which dimension of the experience, if any, the neural signal tracks.
The S/R imaging literature is therefore not merely young; it is structurally underdetermined by its own instruments.
Studies of psychedelic-assisted therapy in patients facing life-threatening illness offer a preliminary window into the neurobiological mechanisms underlying altered states of consciousness.

A systematic review by Ferreira and Reis-Pina (2025) synthesizing six clinical trials (𝑁 = 140 , predominantly oncology patients) reported consistent improvements in spiritual well-being and mystical-type experiences following psilocybin and MDMA-assisted interventions.

Mechanistically, these subjective changes mirror neuroimaging patterns characterized by reduced within-network connectivity, heightened global inter-network communication, and altered thalamic sensory filtering-a profile compatible with cortical entropy and network decoupling models.

Nevertheless, substantial methodological constraints, including small sample cohorts, high overall risk of bias, and functional unblinding driven by prominent psychoactive effects, mean these data serve as hypothesisgenerating insights for human neuroscience rather than established clinical evidence.
Translating altered-state practices into safe clinical practice requires explicit risk management and triage protocols.

Non-pharmacological interventions like breathwork, while mechanistically relevant, induce hyperventilation-mediated hypocapnia that carries genuine risks for patients with cardiac arrhythmias, pregnancy, severe panic disorder, or a lowered seizure threshold.

Additionally, when managing practice-induced or drug-associated adverse events, clinicians require structured routing criteria: persistent depersonalization, hallucinogen persisting perception disorder, or severe psychological crisis warrant formal psychiatric referral, whereas newly emergent focal neurological signs, paroxysmal spells, or unprovoked seizures require an immediate standard epilepsy and neurological workup.
At the level of computational inference, the brain operates as a hierarchical Bayesian prediction engine.
It continuously generates top-down expectations (priors) to interpret incoming sensory and interoceptive data, updating these expectations when prediction errors occur.
Within this framework, "precision weighting" acts as a neuromodulatory gain-control mechanism that adjusts the relative weight assigned to top-down predictions versus incoming sensory evidence.

In non-ordinary experiences (NOEs), this balance shifts: certain states attenuate the influence of top-down expectations, allowing unconstrained sensory and affective signals to dominate awareness, whereas other contexts reinforce top-down predictions.
Non-ordinary states can be elicited through five distinct induction vectors, each operating via a unique primary entry point: 1.
Hypnosis: Operates via sociocognitive suggestion, attenuating voluntary executive control and increasing absorption through top-down frontoparietal modulation.
Meditation: Represents a neuroplastic, training-dependent trajectory where sustained attentional practice gradually alters interoceptive awareness and self-monitoring.

Classical Psychedelics: Act pharmacologically via 5-HT 2A receptor agonism on deep-layer cortical pyramidal neurons, elevating cortical signal entropy and relaxing highlevel narrative priors (the REBUS model).

Voluntary Hyperventilation (Breathwork): Utilizes respiratory mechanicsspecifically transient hypocapnia and reduced arterial CO 2 saturation-to alter autonomic state and induce mystical-type phenomenology.

From a clinical safety perspective, hyperventilation-induced hypocapnia carries specific risks (e.g., lower seizure thresholds, cardiac arrhythmias, or panic decompensation) that require pre-screening.
Focal Neurological Events: Arise from pathological hyper-synchronous epileptic discharges (such as anterior insular ecstatic seizures) or structural lesions.
These organic events must not be assumed to share identical mechanisms with voluntary or pharmacological practices.

A central working hypothesis proposes that despite these disparate entry points, all five vectors may converge on a shared neurodynamic state defined by altered precision weighting and reduced coupling across large-scale intrinsic networks.
Subjectively, this manifests as altered sense of agency, shifting spatiotemporal boundaries, and ego dissolution.
However, this convergence remains an inductive heuristic rather than an established biological reality.
Direct empirical measures of precision weighting currently do not exist for any of these five routes.

Furthermore, existing neuroimaging proxies reveal clear contradictions: meta-analyses in meditation do not demonstrate universal default mode network (DMN) decoupling, nor does hypnosis induce global DMN disintegration.

Addressing the limitations of simple prior-relaxation models, the ALBUS (Altered Beliefs Under Psychedelics) framework demonstrates that top-down expectations are not exclusively relaxed during altered states; they can also be amplified and entrenched through a process termed SEBUS (Strengthened Beliefs Under Psychedelics).
Rather than viewing belief strengthening as an ad-hoc exception, REBUS (relaxation) and SEBUS (strengthening) represent competing parallel computational pathways.

Which pathway dominates is governed downstream by contextual factors: environments characterized by high affective threat, rigid baseline priors, or unsupportive settings trigger reactive SEBUS-type belief hardening to minimize overwhelming prediction error, whereas supportive settings facilitate REBUS-type relaxation.
Pre-specifying these contextual predictors renders the framework empirically falsifiable.

text.text: The Integrative Model: From Triggers to Outcomes
text.formatted: The Integrative Model: From Triggers to Outcomes</head>

text.text: To synthesize mechanistic, phenomenological, and clinical data without theoretical overload, the trajectory of non-ordinary states can be organized into a four-stage master architecture designated as the Trigger-Dynamic Psyche-4E Appraisal-Outcome Model.
Stage 1 encompasses the primary perturbations that disrupt baseline neurodynamics.

These include voluntary contemplative practices such as meditation, ritual, hypnosis, and hyperventilation breathwork; pharmacological agents, principally classical psychedelics; acute boundary events including psychological trauma, near-death experiences, and severe sleep deprivation; and focal organic events such as ecstatic epilepsy or structural brain lesions.
Stage 2 models the acute biological reconfiguration across three mutually constraining operational levels.

At the substrate level ("hardware"), the state is characterized by large-scale network reconfigurations, including variable Default Mode Network (DMN) decoupling, altered triple-network interactions among the DMN, SN, and CEN, reduced thalamic sensory gating, and periaqueductal gray (PAG) recruitment.

At the neuromodulatory-autonomic level ("firmware"), it is defined by altered serotonergic and dopaminergic signaling, elevated cortical signal entropy, shifted salience attribution, altered heart rate variability (HRV/RMSSD), and speculative ponto-geniculo-occipital (PGO) wave activity.

At the computational level ("software"), this dynamic is conceptualized as the attenuation of high-level narrative priors and altered precision weighting, permitting bottomup sensory and affective information to flood conscious awareness.
Stage 3 introduces the 4E Appraisal Prism, operating on the premise that acute neurodynamic shifts do not directly dictate final psychological outcomes.

Instead, these shifts interact bidirectionally with the Prism, which functions as a real-time contextual filter integrating four interdependent facets: embodied (somatic baseline and interoceptive accuracy, such as resting HRV), embedded (physical environment and perceived social safety), enacted (procedural technique, ritual structure, and behavioral framing), and extended (symbolic, cultural, or spiritual cognitive frameworks that assist in sense-making).

When these 4E factors are misaligned-such as through coercive settings, technique overefforting, or destabilizing interpretive frameworks-the Prism operates as a vulnerability matrix that precipitates clinical distress.
Stage 4 resolves these filtered neurodynamic states into three primary outcome trajectories.
Adaptive trajectories manifest as integrated psychological insights, posttraumatic growth, and enhanced spiritual well-being.

Practice-induced adverse trajectories encompass transient or persistent depersonalization, derealization, hallucinogen persisting perception disorder (HPPD), or spiritual crises arising from contextual misalignments.
Primary clinical trajectories involve the acute exacerbation or unmasking of underlying psychiatric disorders, such as primary psychosis or mania.

Clinically, differential triage requires evaluating functional impairment and symptom etiology: persistent functional deficits or severe distress mandate formal psychiatric referral, whereas new-onset focal neurological symptoms, paroxysmal spells, or unprovoked seizures require immediate neurological evaluation and electroencephalographic workup.

Threaded across this entire model is the Epistemological Invariant: identifying the neural mechanisms or computational dynamics of a non-ordinary state does not resolve its ultimate existential or metaphysical validity.

Documenting biological mechanisms, phenomenological reports, and existential meaning as distinct operational domains prevents two clinical errors: reducing meaningful human experiences to simple discharge pathology, and inflating neuroimaging correlates into metaphysical claims.

text.text: Identifying the methodological and theoretical vulnerabilities of a discipline is medically useful only if the diagnosis directly transforms how future clinical trials, observational studies, and neuroimaging paradigms are designed.

In the emerging field of neurospirituality and NOEs, a systematic audit reveals profound structural weaknesses: systematic construct conflation, unvalidated single-item regressors, sample nonindependence-such as the repeated scanning of the Columbia/Weissman multigenerational depression cohort (Weissman et al., 2005; Miller et al., 2014)-and a pervasive habit of driving functional MRI analyses with unvalidated proxies of religiosity.

(2022), out of eighteen neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies examining spirituality, mental health, and neurobiology, thirteen relied on unvalidated single items or external attendance frequency, while only three incorporated psychometrically validated, multidimensional instruments.

text.text: For the clinical neurologist, these are not mere academic quibbles; they represent foundational threats to diagnostic accuracy and mechanistic clarity.

The basic premise of clinical neuroscience holds that valid empirical inferences require valid psychometric constructs, and a body of neuroimaging literature built upon single-item self-reports cannot be salvaged simply by acquiring larger volumes of similarly flawed data.
To establish an empirically defensible framework for neurological practice, future research must systematically address these diagnostic weaknesses through three primary avenues.

First, conceptual conflation-the reflex to mistake a raw, acute phenomenal state for its post-hoc cultural, religious, or psychiatric interpretation-must yield to structured neurophenomenological protocols, deploying standardized clinical interviews with published inter-rater reliability to separate immediate qualitative experiences from downstream narrative appraisals (Timmermann et al., 2023).

text.text: Second, construct validity must become a mandatory inclusion criterion in neuroimaging paradigms, requiring psychometrically validated, multidimensional instruments; no patient or research participant should enter a scanner without such psychometric quantification.

Third, localizationist reductionism must yield to dynamic network neuroscience, resisting the search for hypothetical "spiritual centers" to examine how large-scale systems like the DMN, SN, and CEN interact with subcortical gating structures such as the anterior insula and periaqueductal gray (Picard & Friston, 2014; Unterrainer, 2025).

text.text: Overcoming the clinical translation gap further requires directly addressing widespread sampling biases and longitudinal deficits in the current literature.

The existing evidence base relies disproportionately on small convenience samples from Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic (WEIRD) populations, severely limiting its generalizability to diverse clinical and cross-cultural cohorts (Maraldi et al., 2024; Timmermann et al., 2023).

text.text: Establishing multi-center, cross-cultural research consortia alongside prospective longitudinal designs is essential to track patient trajectories over time, providing the empirical foundation needed to identify the specific baseline variables that moderate whether an acute neurodynamic state resolves into adaptive growth or clinical distress.
As a narrative synthesis based on targeted literature searches rather than an exhaustive systematic review, this paper is subject to potential selection bias and precludes quantitative data pooling.
The generalizability of the underlying empirical literature is further constrained by a heavy reliance on WEIRD study populations, leaving cross-cultural validity unestablished.

Furthermore, widespread publication bias across clinical and contemplative neuroimaging risks overstating regional neural specificity, while clinical trials of psychedelic interventions face significant methodological challenges due to functional unblinding driven by prominent psychoactive effects.

To prevent ad-hoc hedging, address these literature-wide constraints, and maintain a clear distinction between well-replicated data and original conceptual proposals, the claims throughout this synthesis are organized into three explicit epistemic tiers.
Tier 1: Established Empirical Benchmarks.

Replicated findings backed by coordinate-based meta-analyses and validated psychometric instruments, such as core neural networks recruited during meditation, the established factor structures of the Altered States of Consciousness rating scale family (e.g., 3D-ASCr / 5D-ASC), and the four-factor structure of the Revised Mystical Experience Questionnaire (MEQ30).

Tier 2 represents Supported / Preliminary Evidence, consisting of real clinical and physiological findings derived from small-cohort trials, including psychospiritual improvements in psychedelic-assisted palliative care and state shifts induced by hyperventilation-mediated hypocapnia.
Although grounded in empirical data, Tier 2 findings remain qualified by modest sample sizes, heterogeneous control conditions, and unisolated contextual set-and-setting factors.

Tier 3 designates Conceptual & Speculative Heuristics, which gather original theoretical models introduced in this review to structure a fragmented domain, including the six-dimension phenomenological taxonomy, the tri-level neurodynamic architecture ("software," "firmware," "hardware"), the Trigger-Dynamic Psyche-4E Appraisal-Outcome Model, the 4E Appraisal Prism, the five-vector precisionweighting convergence hypothesis, and proposed periaqueductal gray or heart-rate variability mechanisms.

text.text: Crucially, the operational parameters embedded within these Tier 3 frameworksincluding baseline heart-rate variability, interoceptive accuracy tasks, setting inventories, and the six-dimension phenomenological profile-have not yet undergone formal psychometric testing for reliability or prognostic utility.

Furthermore, no empirical study has directly measured precision-weighting shifts across all five induction routes simultaneously, and major interpretive extensions-such as applying predictive processing models (like ALBUS/SEBUS) to non-pharmacological induction vectors or attributing central valencedetermining roles to periaqueductal gray signaling-remain unverified hypotheses.
Finally, as a single-author synthesis reconciling disciplines of vastly different methodological maturities, theoretical integration inevitably reflects specific interpretive decisions.

Explicitly categorizing these frameworks into Tier 3 ensures that clinicians and neuroscientists can utilize them as testable research heuristics for prospective inquiry without mistaking speculative formulations for established diagnostic tools or confirmed pathophysiology.

This work provides general neurologists with a practical, non-reductionist framework for evaluating Non-Ordinary Experiences (NOEs)-states characterized by altered selfawareness, temporal perception, or spatial boundaries arising from contemplative practices, psychoactive substances, or focal neurological events.

The overarching synthesis connects three conceptual heuristics: a six-dimension phenomenological taxonomy for mapping firstperson reports of what an experience was like, independent of any downstream interpretation; a tri-level descriptive taxonomy contrasting normal and non-ordinary states across computational inference, neuromodulatory-autonomic state-setting, and large-scale network substrates; and the master Trigger-Dynamic Psyche-4E Appraisal-Outcome Model, a process architecture in which acute triggers perturb neurodynamics across the tri-level taxonomy, the resulting dynamics unfold within the patient's psyche, and long-term trajectories toward adaptive growth or clinical distress are selected by the patient's bodily state, social setting, technique, and interpretive beliefs (the 4E Appraisal Prism).

Notably, the six-dimension schema extends the foundational phenomenological framework established by Timmermann et al. (2023), and it functions within the model as the descriptive language for characterizing the Dynamic Psyche stage-the experiential state that lies between trigger and appraisal.

text.text: Two primary hypotheses anchor this theoretical framework, neither of which is yet empirically established: first, the Precision-Weighting Convergence Hypothesis, which posits that five distinct induction routes (meditation, 5-HT2A classical psychedelics, hypocapnic circular breathwork, hypnosis, and focal insular seizures) share a common neurodynamic shift toward reduced top-down prior precision and large-scale network decoupling (Carhart-Harris & Friston, 2019; Havenith et al., 2025; Picard & Friston, 2014; Timmermann et al., 2023), although direct computational measurements across all five vectors are lacking and network findings remain inconsistent across modalities (Baten et al., 2026); and second, the Contextual Outcome-Mediation Claim, which asserts that acute neural perturbations do not independently dictate long-term results, but rather whether an experience resolves into integrated growth or triggers depersonalization, hallucinogen persisting perception disorder (HPPD), or spiritual crisis depends on contextual filtering via the 4E Appraisal Prism.

text.text: Three falsifiable predictions follow from these frameworks: first (P1), first-person NOE reports decompose into the hypothesized six latent dimensions rather than a different latent structure; second (P2), baseline 4E appraisal variables statistically mediate the triggeroutcome relationship above trigger intensity alone; and third (P3), the five induction vectors exhibit a convergent shift in precision-weighting proxies.
The failure of any of these predictions in prospective testing would refute the corresponding framework.
Methodological rigor must be applied symmetrically across the discipline.

text.text: The six-step clinical reasoning heuristic offers a research-stage tool that walks the clinician through the model in practice: phenomenological profiling across the six dimensions, trigger identification, 4E appraisal analysis, dynamics and controllability, functional impact, and risk screening-guiding appropriate clinical routing or integration support.
At the core of this framework is a fundamental distinction: brain biology, subjective experiences, and personal meanings are three separate levels of analysis.
Describing the neural activity associated with a transcendent state clarifies its physical substrate without reducing its personal meaning or proving metaphysical claims.
Maintaining this distinction prevents both the reflexive pathologization of adaptive experiences and the romanticization of underlying neurological disease.
